title: First light: Hera resolves two asteroids instead of one

content:
The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft for planetary defense has resolved its two target asteroids separately for the first time, revealing the binary nature of the Didymos system, currently some 197 million km (122 ...

Hera imaged Didymos and Dimorphos with its monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera on the evening of Friday, Oct. 18, at a distance of 1,280 km (795 miles) from the asteroid pair.

"With this image the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," explains Michael Kueppers. "Before this acquisition the spacecraft was still resolving the Didymos system as a single dot. But now, even though Dimorphos is made up of only around one pixel in this initial image, it is clearly well separated from its parent body."

This first image came following the success of Hera's braking maneuvers earlier this month. A pair of thruster firings a week apart slowed the spacecraft to just 20 m/s (45 miles per hour) relative to its two target asteroids, allowing it to come gradually closer on a fine-tuned basis.

At 151 m (495 feet) across, Dimorphos is about the size of the Great Pyramid of Giza, while the 780-m-diameter (2,560-foot-diameter) Didymos asteroid is a little smaller than Dubai's Burj Khalifa skyscraper, the tallest building in the world. The pair orbit an average 1.15 km (0.71 miles) apart from each other, with Dimorphos orbiting its parent at about 18 cm/s (7.1 inches per second).

Asteroid Didymos (bottom left) and its moonlet, Dimorphos, about 2.5 minutes before the impact of NASA's DART spacecraft. Credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins APL
